purpose: Unreleased doctrinal discriminators for the affinity expansion review. These questions are not in a public route, interpretation rule, or affinity catalog. Existing construct targets are navigation metadata, not permission to infer a tradition.
itemIdPolicy: Permanent IDs use <domain>I<3 digits>. IDs are never reused after retirement.

items.text: Suppose breaking a well-justified rule in one case would clearly produce the best overall outcome, without weakening the rule for anyone else. What ultimately determines whether this act is right?

options.label: The consequences of this particular act.
Whether it follows a rule justified by the consequences of generally following it.
Whether it honors a duty that is not ultimately justified by consequences.
No single one of these always determines rightness.

items.notes: Act-outcome favors a narrow act-consequentialist criterion; rule-outcome favors rule consequentialism; rule-independent opposes both. This is about rightness, not the best everyday decision procedure. One answer is not independent corroboration.

items.text: What ultimately justifies a moral rule against harming an innocent person?

options.label: Following that rule generally produces better consequences than the alternatives.
A person's claim against being harmed can constrain us independently of the rule's overall consequences.
The rule is justified by principles affected people could reasonably accept.
More than one of these can justify the rule without any one being ultimate.

items.notes: General-consequences is a candidate rule-consequentialist ground. A person can endorse a useful rule without treating consequences as its ultimate justification. The agreement option is not automatically Scanlonian.

items.text: When comparing possible outcomes morally, what can make one outcome better in itself?

options.label: Only how well the people affected fare; other features matter through their effect on people's welfare.
People's welfare matters, but justice or other values can improve an outcome independently of welfare.
Some rights or duties matter morally without making the outcome itself better.
None of these fits my view.

items.notes: Welfare-only concerns outcome value, not act rightness or maximization. It therefore cannot alone establish utilitarianism. The rights-priority answer may coexist with welfare-only outcome value.

items.text: Two available actions affect everyone's welfare. One produces more total welfare; the other respects a promise but produces less total welfare. Assume no other effects differ. What determines which action is morally right?

options.label: The action producing the most total welfare is right.
Keeping the promise can be right even when it produces less total welfare.
The welfare difference is a strong reason, but it does not by itself settle which action is right.
None of these fits my view.

items.notes: Maximize-welfare is compatible with act utilitarianism in this case but does not distinguish all act and rule forms; combine only with an independently reviewed criterion. The vignette fixes aggregate welfare, not distribution, and should be comprehension-reviewed.

items.text: Before acting on a personal rule, should a person ask whether everyone could follow that same rule without making an exception for themselves?

options.label: Yes; being able to adopt the rule consistently for everyone is part of what makes the act right.
Yes as a useful check, but it does not determine rightness.
Only if doing so tends to improve outcomes.
No general test like this is required.

items.notes: Constitutive option bears on a Kantian universal-law reading; generic consistency or a heuristic alone does not establish Kantian ethics. Scholarly variants of the categorical imperative require review.

items.text: Could an action be wrong because it treats a person merely as a tool for others, even if it would produce a greater total benefit?

options.label: Yes; the person's standing can rule it out independently of the total benefit.
Usually, but only because that treatment tends to have bad consequences.
No; if it really produces the greatest overall benefit, that determines rightness.
It depends on what the person consented to and how they are treated.

items.notes: A yes answer also fits non-Kantian rights views. It is a discriminator against unrestricted aggregation, not a standalone Kantian classification.

items.text: For a morally difficult action, what is the deepest question to settle first?

options.label: What a person of good character would do as part of living well.
Which duty or rule applies to the act.
Which choice produces the best overall outcome.
None of these is generally prior to the others.

items.notes: The first option prioritizes virtue and flourishing in practical explanation; merely admiring good character does not. Does not settle which school of virtue ethics applies.

items.text: Two people have equal urgent need, but one depends on you through an ongoing caring relationship. Could that relationship itself give you a moral reason to help that person first?

options.label: Yes; responding to dependence within the relationship is itself part of what morality asks.
Yes, but only because I previously accepted a role or duty.
Only if helping that person has better consequences.
No; the equal needs give them equal claims regardless of the relationship.

items.notes: Separates care as a moral ground from prior role duty, outcome calculation, and equal need. Existing NEI028 asks whether the relationship gives an additional reason; this draft is only useful if that answer fails to distinguish the ground, so review for redundancy before release.

items.text: A policy gives many people small benefits while imposing a serious avoidable burden on one person. What most directly explains why it may be wrong?

options.label: The burdened person could reasonably reject the policy as a rule for everyone, even if the small benefits add up to more.
It is wrong only if the total harm outweighs the combined benefits.
It is wrong if the parties could agree on another policy that serves each person's interests better.
More than one consideration matters, with no single one decisive.

items.notes: Near existing NEI031; the explicit aggregate and mutual-advantage alternatives are the only added discrimination. If existing NEI031 already does this adequately, retire this draft. Reasonable rejection alone is not every form of contractualism.

items.text: A person is wise, just, and courageous but suffers illness and poverty through no fault of their own. Which claim best fits your view of that person's life?

options.label: Their virtue is the only genuine good; illness and poverty can be disfavored without diminishing that good.
Virtue matters greatly, but illness and poverty can also make the life worse in themselves.
How well the person fares matters more than virtue in assessing their life.
None of these fits my view.

items.notes: Targets the Stoic virtue-only-good thesis, not emotional restraint. The exact academic basis is recorded in the proposed source claim. This single commitment cannot establish the whole Stoic philosophy; the wording of good versus welfare needs comprehension review.

items.text: Suppose people use an ideal process of fair, informed reasoning to settle a moral disagreement. What role could the result of that process have?

options.label: Under suitable conditions, it can help constitute the correct moral standard.
It can help discover a moral standard that is correct independently of any such process.
It can produce agreement without making or finding a correct moral standard.
Its role depends on the kind of moral question.

items.notes: Constitution differs from discovery and mere agreement. 'Suitable conditions' leaves schools of constructivism unresolved; no single procedure or universal constructivist identity follows.

items.text: Which description of mind and body is closest to your view?

options.label: Mental states are wholly physical, even if physical explanations can be complex.
Mental and physical features are both real, and at least some mental features are fundamentally nonphysical.
Reality is fundamentally mental; physical things depend on mind in some way.
Present physical explanations are incomplete, but I am unsure what follows about reality.

items.notes: Two-kinds supports a broad property-or-substance dualist contrast but does not settle which dualism. Unexplained resists the false positive from an explanatory gap. Mental-fundamental is only a provisional idealist signal.

items.text: Which claim best describes how conscious experience is distributed in nature?

options.label: Experience itself is a basic and widespread feature of nature.
Non-experiential precursors may be basic and widespread, while experience arises only in some systems.
Experience arises only in some sufficiently complex systems.
A very simple system might experience something, but that would not make experience fundamental or widespread.
I do not have a settled view.

items.notes: Distinguishes panpsychism from panprotopsychism, complexity-only views, and MSI015’s mere possibility of simple-system experience. The status of a putative precursor remains a specialist review point.

items.text: What authority should a competent adult normally have over their own body?

options.label: They have a strong claim to decide its use and to refuse others' demands, subject to the same claims of others.
They have substantial control, but others' needs can sometimes justify requiring their labor.
Collective decisions may direct a person’s bodily choices for shared ends under suitable conditions.
The answer depends too much on the circumstances for a general claim.

items.notes: Robust option is relevant to bodily self-ownership, not sufficient for either left or right libertarianism. Control over labor and transfer rights remain separately unmeasured.

items.text: A previously unused natural resource is claimed for private use without anyone's consent. What condition, if any, is needed for that claim to be just?

options.label: Peaceful first use can create a strong private claim without owing others a share of the resource's value.
Private use can be allowed, but others retain an equal claim to the resource's value or a fair share of natural resources.
Private use requires authorization by a community that retains collective control.
No one principle covers all such resources.

items.notes: Directly contrasts right- and left-libertarian resource principles without inferring either from generic redistribution skepticism. First-use wording may conflate competing right-libertarian acquisition theories; review before route inclusion.

items.text: Who should normally have effective control over major productive assets such as factories and large firms?

options.label: The workers who use them, through institutions they can genuinely govern.
The wider public, through institutions it can genuinely govern.
State officials, even if workers or the public have little control over decisions.
Private owners, within general rules protecting workers and others.
Different forms should coexist without one general default.

items.notes: Worker-governed and publicly governed answers are distinct social-control possibilities; state ownership without effective social control is not sufficient. This does not decide markets versus planning or democratic governance.

items.text: A country can prevent a serious harm abroad at modest cost, but its citizens gain nothing in return. What gives it a political reason to act?

options.label: People beyond its borders can have claims on its institutions independently of national benefit.
Helping is admirable, but foreign people have no claim on its institutions.
It has a political reason to act only if citizens will benefit through reciprocity or security.
The reason depends on the kind of harm and the institution's mandate.

items.notes: Distinguishes institutional claim from humanitarian permission and instrumental national benefit. Existing PLI020 and PLI067 touch similar cases; review local dependence before release.

items.text: If no state held exclusive authority to enforce law, which institution, if any, should ordinarily provide courts and protection?

options.label: Competing providers chosen through property, contract, and voluntary exchange.
Community associations organized without making protection a market service.
A single public authority should be established instead.
Several forms could be legitimate; no one form is generally required.

items.notes: Conditional premise distinguishes forms of stateless order. Market-providers alone cannot infer anarchism without a separately established state-abolition commitment; community associations do not by themselves establish social anarchism.

items.text: Suppose an ecosystem could be damaged without causing suffering or loss to any person or animal. Could the ecosystem itself still give us a moral reason not to damage it?

options.label: Yes; the ecological whole can matter morally in its own right.
Only individual living beings could supply that reason, not the ecosystem as a whole.
Only effects on present or future humans could supply that reason.
I am unsure whether an ecosystem itself can matter morally.

items.notes: Separates ecological-whole moral standing from animal-focused and human-centered environmental concern. The proposed SEP source claim is philosophical context, not an item-validation study.

items.text: Do all justified beliefs about the world ultimately need support from some beliefs that are justified without depending on further beliefs?

options.label: Yes; some basic beliefs must stop a regress of reasons.
No; beliefs can be justified by how they support one another within a coherent network.
No; justification can continue through an open-ended chain of reasons.
I am unsure what ultimately supports justified beliefs.

items.notes: Tests the broader regress thesis beyond one perceptual or intuitive starting point. Yes_basic does not specify which beliefs are basic or settle debates about coherentism.

items.text: Suppose every choice is fully determined by earlier events. Which claim about freedom and responsibility is closest to your view?

options.label: Some determined choices can still be genuinely free and morally responsible.
Some determined choices can be genuinely free, but not deserving of basic moral blame.
A person may deserve moral blame, but determined choices are not genuinely free.
Determined choices are neither genuinely free nor a basis for basic moral blame.

items.notes: Separates compatibility of freedom from compatibility of moral responsibility. Do not infer actual determinism from a conditional answer or treat responsibility-only as an ordinary compatibilist freedom view.

items.text: Imagine a person raised with entirely different relationships and social roles but the same bodily traits. Which description best fits how those changes affect who the person is?

options.label: Those relationships and roles partly constitute who the person is.
They strongly influence the person, but identity is ultimately fixed by features within the individual.
They may affect behavior but little of the person’s identity.
There is no general answer across kinds of identity.

items.notes: Separates constitutive relational selfhood from the causal influence or personal value of relationships. This does not establish a single cross-cultural self theory.

items.text: Which statement best fits your view about a deity with intentions or purposes?

options.label: At least one such deity exists.
A divine reality exists, but none is a deity with intentions or purposes.
Such a deity may exist, but I do not affirm that one does.
No divine reality exists.

items.notes: Combines existence and agentic character in one referent. Conditional RCI025 alone cannot establish personal theism, and a possible deity is not an affirmed deity.

items.text: Which statement best fits your view about a deity that acts in ordinary events?

options.label: A deity exists and sometimes acts in ordinary events.
A deity exists but does not intervene in ordinary events.
A deity might intervene, but I do not affirm that such a deity exists.
No deity exists.

items.notes: Links the intervention claim to the affirmed deity rather than to supernatural possibility in general. Does not by itself establish a miracle or particular religious tradition.

items.text: Which description best fits your present view about whether any deity exists?

options.label: I believe at least one exists.
I believe none exists.
I have considered the question and suspend judgment.
I have not considered the question enough to form a view.
I am unsure what the question means or what would count as a deity.

items.notes: Separates considered suspension from mere lack of exposure or unclear terms. This is a respondent stance, not a claim that the matter is unknowable.
